A Scientific Claim Stability Framework for Evaluating MRI Morphometry Pipelines
summary: MRI morphometry pipelines are often evaluated by measurement agreement or downstream accuracy, yet their scientific value depends on the conclusions they support. Two pipelines can produce similar feature-level results yet support different conclusions about aging, cognitive decline, or neurodegeneration. We introduce Scientific Claim Stability (SCS), a claim-centric evaluation framework that converts region-of-interest (ROI) morphometry tables into auditable claim cards and evaluates their support under changes in dataset, processing pipeline, atlas, feature family, and target. Across 10,370 MRI scans from three datasets and five cohorts, SCS generates 2,783 claim cards and evaluates 89 claim-family pairs. The evaluation distinguishes stable, transferable, and fragile claims. FreeSurfer 8-FastSurfer comparisons show high evidence concordance and low anatomical-support overlap under the primary covariate specification. Acquisition-adjusted analyses show that the magnitude of support disagreement depends on the model specification. Structured review by specialists in geriatrics, neuroscience, and radiology, alongside auxiliary ChatGPT and Gemini reviewers, assesses claim plausibility, clarity, faithfulness, usefulness, and caution. SCS provides a reproducible way to audit the evidential stability of morphometry claims without assuming a universal gold standard.

title: Homoharringtonine targets XPC to inhibit DNA damage repair and sensitize tumors to platinum-based chemotherapy
summary: DNA damage repair (DDR) is essential for preserving genomic stability and also represents a key targetable axis in cancer drug development. Here, we identify and validate homoharringtonine (HHT), a clinically approved antileukemic drug, as a novel DDR inhibitor using a phenotype-driven, high-content screen based on 53BP1 Tudor-domain foci formation. Mechanistically, HHT directly binds XPC, a critical nucleotide excision repair (NER) factor, with high affinity (Kd = 158.4 nM) in a manner dependent on Thr795 of XPC. HHT disrupts XPC-damaged DNA binding, impairs NER, and reduces non-homologous end joining (NHEJ) efficiency. Consequently, HHT sensitizes tumor cells to platinum-based chemotherapy in vitro and in vivo. These findings establish a phenotype-based platform for DDR inhibitor discovery, identify HHT as a first-in-class XPC inhibitor and uncover a previously unrecognized mechanism of HHT that may be exploited to enhance platinum-based therapy in solid tumors.

title: Plasma untargeted metabolomics reveals distinct metabolic disturbances between sexes following inhalation of ultrafine particles and exposure to aircraft noise in mice
summary: Traffic noise and air pollution, particularly ultrafine particles (UFP), are significantly associated with health risks. However, the systemic metabolic consequences of the combined effects of UFP and aircraft noise (AN) exposure on health remain poorly understood. We aimed to investigate changes in plasma metabolites in healthy wildtype C57BL/6J mice following whole-body inhalation exposure to UFP (average diameter <40 nm), AN and their combination (UFP+AN). Liquid chromatography-mass spectrometry (LC-MS)-based untargeted plasma metabolomics analysis was undertaken for UFP, AN, and combined UFP+AN-exposed mice of both sexes. This study identified a total of 1146 plasma metabolites. Across exposure groups, AN induced the greatest plasma metabolomic changes in both sexes, while UFP significantly altered metabolites only in females, indicating a sex-specific response. The combined UFP+AN exposure produced a modestly enhanced effect in males compared with either single exposure but showed an attenuated effect in females. Pathway analyses revealed that lipid and amino acid metabolism were the most affected, followed by xenobiotics, and cofactors and vitamins, after exposure in both female and male mice. Additionally, in the clean air control group, we identified sex differences in 49 plasma metabolites, which mostly included lipids and amino acids. Following exposure, however, sex-dependent metabolic differences became more pronounced and exposure-specific, suggesting that UFP and AN have distinct effects on plasma metabolome of male and female mice that extend beyond baseline sexual dimorphism observed in unexposed animals. To our knowledge, this study is the first comprehensive characterization of systemic metabolic changes in mice after combination of UFP and AN exposure, providing new insight into the interplay between traffic noise and air pollution health risks.

title: Oleic acid suppresses NLRP3 inflammasome activation to prevent dermal macrophage death and limit imiquimod-induced psoriasis
summary: Psoriasis is associated with altered lipid metabolism, including reduced expression of fatty acid metabolism genes and decreased circulating oleic acid. Here we report that oral oleic acid supplementation normalized serum oleic acid levels and protected from skin thickening and epidermal hyperplasia in a imiquimod mice model of psoriasis. These effects were associated with preserved skin-resident macrophage numbers and reduced expression of key psoriasis-associated inflammatory markers. Mechanistically, imiquimod induces dermal macrophage death via NLRP3/caspase-1 inflammasome activation, while adoptive transfer of dermal macrophages attenuates psoriasiform inflammation. Oleic acid rescued macrophages from imiquimod and nigericin-induced death in vitro by suppressing NF-{kappa}B and NLRP3/caspase-1 signaling, lowering IL-1{beta} and reactive oxygen species production, and restoring mitochondrial homeostasis, independently of TLR7. Together, our results position dermal macrophage survival as a previously unrecognized checkpoint in psoriasiform inflammation, and suggest that restoring lipid metabolic fitness, rather than solely targeting downstream inflammatory mediators, may offer an additional mechanism-based strategy to limit tissue- damaging inflammation.

title: Neuronal and glial transcriptional states vary with proximity to tangle-bearing neurons in the human entorhinal cortex
summary: More neurons die in Alzheimer's disease than form tangles, and tangle-bearing neurons can persist for decades, so tangles alone cannot explain degeneration. We combined 6,000-plex spatial transcriptomics with PHF1 immunofluorescence (167,176 cells; 9 donors) and imaging mass cytometry (170,195 cells; 62 donors), measuring each cell's distance to the nearest tangle. Tangle-bearing layer 2-3 excitatory neurons were enriched late along a trajectory of increasing microtubule-associated, synaptic and V-ATPase expression, with elevated p62 and K48-ubiquitin. Tangle-free neurons shared more of this state the closer they lay to a tangle, including higher chaperone and autophagy scores, p62 and nuclear size. Nearby glia had higher disease-associated scores, with astrocytes expressing less GFAP. Excitatory, but not inhibitory, neuron loss was greatest in subtypes closest to tangles and cortical depths richest in phosphorylated tau. Selective neuronal vulnerability may reflect not only a neuron's susceptibility to forming a tangle but also where it lies relative to one.
